title: The pre-sale model, before and after
note: The before column is the mainland pre-sale (期房) model as it actually operates. The after column is the same model with Kirim between the bank and the developer. Nothing about selling off-plan changes — only what the money is allowed to do while the buyer waits.

before.label: China pre-sale today
before.sub: 期房 · off-plan sale, money released by approval

steps.text: Obtains a pre-sale permit and sells the tower off-plan, years before it exists.
Pays a deposit — commonly 20–30% of the price — against a flat that is a drawing.
Disburses the entire mortgage to the developer up front, in one payment.
The money nominally sits in a local pre-sale supervision account at a designated bank.
A local official approves each draw. The rules differ city by city and enforcement is uneven.
In practice, cash is moved to land purchases, other projects, and group debt.
Funding runs out. Work slows, then stops. The tower stands unfinished.
Keeps repaying a mortgage on a home that does not exist, with no way to stop.
Litigation, a mortgage payment strike, or a state rescue fund — years, not weeks.

after.label: The same sale, with Kirim
after.sub: off-plan sale, money released by evidence

steps.text: Obtains a pre-sale permit and sells the tower off-plan.
Pays a deposit against a flat that is still a drawing.
Disburses the entire mortgage on day one — into escrow, not to the developer.
steps.changed: The developer is no longer the recipient. Same money, same day, different destination.

steps.text: One escrow per construction stage, each locked under a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 condition.
steps.changed: There is no approver to lobby. Without the preimage, nobody can move it — Kirim included.

steps.text: Reaches a stage and submits evidence: geotagged photographs, delivery notes, permits.
steps.changed: A draw is now a claim that has to survive examination, not a form to be stamped.

steps.text: Buys the verification it needs — inspection, carrier, supplier registry — paying per call over x402.
steps.changed: The agent pays for its own facts. Nobody has to send a person to site to move US$40,000.

steps.text: Runs thirteen deterministic checks. Conforming evidence releases that stage in about four seconds.
steps.changed: Release is a rule, not a relationship. The same evidence gets the same answer every time.

steps.text: Non-conforming evidence releases nothing, and the buyer is shown the check that failed.
steps.changed: The failure is legible on the day it happens, not two years later when the crane leaves.

steps.text: A stage never reached expires: CancelAfter returns that stage's money to the buyer.
steps.changed: Refund without litigation. The unbuilt half was never the developer's to lose.

steps.text: Every completed stage is written to the developer's own XRPL account as a credential.
steps.changed: A developer who builds carries the proof with them to the next project.

comparison.q: Can the developer sell before completion?
comparison.before: Yes — off-plan sale is the norm.

comparison.q: Does the buyer start paying before completion?
comparison.before: Yes — deposit, then mortgage instalments begin.

comparison.q: Where does the mortgage money go?
comparison.before: Straight to the developer, in full, on day one.
comparison.after: Into per-stage XRPL escrow, in full, on day one.
comparison.delta: The bank still pays immediately. The developer just is not who receives it.

comparison.q: Where does the buyer's money sit?
comparison.before: A local pre-sale supervision account, drawn down on an official's approval.
comparison.after: An escrow object on a public ledger, drawn down on a crypto-condition.
comparison.delta: Discretion is replaced by a condition. Anyone can read the balance; nobody can lobby it.

comparison.q: Can the developer use the money elsewhere?
comparison.before: In practice, yes — diversion to other projects and group debt is routine.
comparison.after: No. Not for one stage, not for one hour.
comparison.delta: This is the whole change. Everything else follows from it.

comparison.before: The buyer — a mortgage on a flat that may never be built.
comparison.after: Nobody carries it, because unbuilt stages are never released.
comparison.delta: Risk is not transferred to an insurer. It is removed from the transaction.

comparison.q: What happens if the developer runs out of cash?
comparison.before: Work stops, buyers keep paying, recovery takes years of litigation.
comparison.after: Remaining stages expire and return to the buyer automatically.
comparison.delta: The buyer's downside stops at the stages that were actually built.
